parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a member of the platform's airspace desk. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift until you hand over and leave?
I don't know.
To make it easier, what is the very first thing you do when you sit down at the airspace desk for your shift?
I don't know.
Think back to your most recent shift—what was a specific task or problem you dealt with that day?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which involves working with the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
Could you give me a concrete example of a recent closure you entered, and how you went about finding out how much disruption it caused?
I don't know.
What does "disruption" mean in your work—what exact numbers or facts do you look at to measure it?
I don't know.
Who gives you the information about closures, flight corridors, and zones, and who do you pass information on to?

The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce closures, which can be planned ones with a start and end time or sudden ones that apply at once. Closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations.
Do the customer companies ever send requests or information to you, such as asking for new flight corridors or sites?
I don't know.
When a sudden closure is announced or amended by the authorities, what do you need to know right away?
A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
Since you cannot look into any single company's operations, what information *are* you allowed to see to know how much disruption a closure caused while drones are in the air?
I don't know.
What was the worst day you've had at the airspace desk in the last few months, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
What is the hardest or most stressful situation you have to deal with when managing closures and corridors?
A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
